previous_disclosures.section: CONSOLIDATED RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > 2023 compared with 2022
previous_disclosures.summary: Investment banking fees decreased in 2023 compared with 2022, primarily due to lower advisory fees from reduced transaction activity and lower debt underwriting fees, which were partially offset by higher equity underwriting fees.

Investment Banking revenue was $6.2 billion, down 4%; excluding $257 million of markdowns in 2022, it was down 8%, driven by lower advisory and debt underwriting fees, partially offset by higher equity underwriting fees. The firm ranked #1 for Global Investment Banking fees according to Dealogic.

Debt underwriting fees were $2.6 billion, down 8%, as challenging market conditions, primarily in the first half of the year, resulted in lower issuance activity across leveraged loans, investment-grade loans, and high-grade bonds, largely offset by higher issuance activity in high-yield bonds.

Equity underwriting fees were $1.2 billion, up 11%, driven by higher levels of follow-on offerings due to lower equity market volatility and higher convertible securities offerings, partially offset by lower private placement activity.

current_disclosures.section: BUSINESS SEGMENT & CORPORATE RESULTS > 2024 compared with 2023
current_disclosures.summary: Banking & Payments revenue was $35.3 billion, up 11%, driven by Investment Banking fees up 37% (ranked #1 globally), Payments revenue up 1% despite margin compression from higher rates, and Lending revenue up 8% due to higher rates and the First Republic acquisition.

comparisons.peer_topic: Investment Banking Fee Performance and Drivers
comparisons.peer_summary: Total Corporation investment banking fees increased 31 percent to $6.2 billion compared to the same period in 2023, primarily driven by higher debt and equity issuance fees and higher advisory fees.
comparisons.comparison: Similar to JPMorgan's report of favorable market conditions driving fee increases, Bank of America's Global Banking and Global Markets investment banking fees increased 31% to $6.2 billion. This growth was primarily driven by the same three factors identified by JPMorgan: higher debt and equity issuance fees and higher advisory fees. Both disclosures highlight a broad-based recovery or boom in capital markets activities.

comparisons.peer_summary: Investment Banking revenues increased 38%, fueled by a 42% rise in fees from rebounding wallet activity and gains across products, including a 61% increase in DCM underwriting fees due to record debt issuance and a 38% increase in equity underwriting fees from stronger follow-on and convertibles activity.
comparisons.comparison: Citigroup and JPMorgan both attribute their 2024 investment banking revenue growth to favorable market conditions and specific product strength. JPMorgan cites 'favorable market conditions' leading to higher debt, equity, and advisory fees. Citigroup mirrors this by citing a 'rebound in overall wallet activity' and 'wallet share gains across all products.' Both firms highlight significant growth in debt underwriting (JPMorgan: leveraged/high-grade/high-yield bonds; Citigroup: DCM up 61% from record issuance) and equity underwriting (JPMorgan: IPOs/follow-ons; Citigroup: equity up 38% from follow-ons/convertibles). Citigroup explicitly quantifies the 42% increase in fees, while JPMorgan focuses on the volume drivers.

sentences.text: Investment banking fees increased, reflecting in CIB the benefit of favorable market conditions, which resulted in:
• higher debt underwriting fees predominantly driven by higher industry-wide issuances in leveraged loans, and in high-grade and high-yield bonds,
• higher equity underwriting fees driven by higher industry-wide fees and wallet share gains in IPOs, and in follow-on and convertible securities offerings, and
• higher advisory fees driven by higher industry-wide mergers and acquisitions ("M&A") activity and wallet share gains.
Investment Banking revenues increased 38%, reflecting a 42% increase in investment banking fees, due to a rebound in overall wallet activity and wallet share gains across all products.
DCM underwriting fees increased 61%, benefiting from near record debt issuance, particularly in investment grade and higher leveraged finance activity.
Advisory fees increased 22%, due to strong announced deal volume from earlier in the year coming to fruition as those transactions closed.
Equity underwriting fees increased 38%, due to stronger follow-on and convertibles activity.

comparisons.peer_summary: Investment banking revenues were $7.74 billion in 2024, up 24% from 2023, primarily due to significantly higher revenues in debt underwriting (leveraged finance) and equity underwriting (secondary and IPOs), as well as higher advisory revenues from increased M&A activity.
comparisons.comparison: Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan both report significant increases in investment banking revenues driven by similar specific segments. JPMorgan notes higher debt underwriting fees from leveraged loans/bonds and higher equity underwriting fees from IPOs. Goldman Sachs similarly attributes its 24% revenue increase to significantly higher debt underwriting driven by leveraged finance and equity underwriting driven by secondary and IPO offerings. Both firms also report higher advisory revenues linked to increased M&A activity, although Goldman Sachs explicitly states industry-wide M&A volumes remained below historical averages while debt volumes increased significantly, a nuance JPMorgan captures by attributing its advisory gains to 'higher industry-wide mergers and acquisitions activity'.

comparisons.peer_topic: Investment Banking Revenue Growth and Drivers
comparisons.peer_summary: Investment banking net revenues increased 35% to $6,170 million in 2024, driven by higher M&A advisory volumes, increased equity underwriting from IPOs and follow-ons, and higher fixed income underwriting from bond and loan issuances.
comparisons.comparison: Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan both attribute their 2024 investment banking revenue growth to a broad-based increase in advisory, equity underwriting, and fixed income/debt underwriting. Morgan Stanley reports a 35% increase driven by higher completed M&A transactions, higher IPOs/follow-ons, and higher bond/loan issuances. JPMorgan similarly attributes its increase to higher debt underwriting (leveraged loans/bonds), equity underwriting (IPOs/follow-ons), and advisory fees (M&A). Both disclosures highlight the same three core drivers of investment banking fee growth in 2024.
